blocks.title: Honors — carry the model to the asteroid
blocks.markdown: You can now solve a constant-acceleration problem. The honors demand isn't another plug-in — it's dropping that model onto a problem you haven't seen, the one the whole year is about.

blocks.whatWeKnow: We have the kinematic equations for constant acceleration and we can choose the right one and defend the choice.
blocks.connection: A deflection plan would give 2026-XJ a small, steady push — a constant acceleration — over a long time. Today you reason about whether that's even enough to matter, using only Unit 1's tools, and you name what those tools still can't answer.

blocks.frame: Using $\Delta x = v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$, a tiny steady acceleration over a long time produces ___, which is why ___. But Unit 1 alone cannot tell me ___, because ___.
blocks.prompt: TRANSFER: Suppose a thruster could give 2026-XJ a tiny but constant sideways acceleration for the entire year before arrival. Using constant-acceleration reasoning (not a memorized number), explain why even a small acceleration applied over a very long time can build into a meaningful sideways displacement. Then name ONE thing Unit 1's kinematics still CANNOT answer about this deflection — and which later idea (force? mass thrown off? energy?) would be needed to answer it.

blocks.title: Close forward
blocks.markdown: Kinematics tells us *what a motion does* if we already know the acceleration. It never tells us **what causes** that acceleration, or how big a push it takes to produce it. That 'how big a push?' question is the door into the next unit — Newton's laws and $F = ma$. The deflection story is just getting started.
